description: Compare any number of clusters of one experiment: a leaderboard and distributions over each cluster's own active window, an elapsed-time overlay, a timeline and the experiment's report, then the per-cluster sections over the experiment's span. Latency comes from the OpenTelemetry JMX agent as pre-aggregated per-node percentiles, so cluster-level latency panels report the slowest node rather than a re-aggregated quantile. To compare two clusters exactly, open the cluster pair.

panels.title: Leaderboard: each cluster over its own active window

panels.description: One row per selected cluster, each figure over that cluster's own active window: the time it served client requests, found at the Resolution step within the experiment's span. Values are raw. Read p99 and write p99 are the slowest node's. CPU busy covers every host of the cluster. Throughput CV is the standard deviation of throughput over its mean. Sort by any header. Colours run per column, green for the better end. Started is in UTC. The Cluster links open System Overview and Cassandra Overview on the cluster's window, the cluster pair with this cluster as A, and the report of the selected experiment.

Select one experiment to see its report: with All there is no single report and the frame shows the documents server's error page. Upload a report with easy-db-lab report upload DIR.
panels.title: Report: ${experiment:text}
1. Fleet Snapshot — Current health at a glance across all clusters

panels.description: One row per cluster: write throughput, the ${percentile} write and read latency of the slowest node in that cluster, and the error rate. Cassandra emits its percentiles pre-aggregated per node, so there is no cluster-wide percentile to compute; the slowest node is the honest cluster-level summary. Latency thresholds assume milliseconds.
panels.title: Cluster Summary
3. Errors — Error trends and windowed incident history

panels.description: Write failures and timeouts per cluster over time. One line per cluster per error type.
panels.title: Failures, Timeouts + Unavailables

panels.description: Each row is one cluster. Red segments indicate time windows with non-zero errors. Best for identifying which cluster had incidents and when.
panels.title: Error Events by Cluster

panels.description: Slowest node in each cluster at ${percentile}. Cassandra now reports this percentile pre-aggregated, straight from the EstimatedHistogram reservoir on each node. Pre-aggregated percentiles cannot be recombined into a true cluster-wide percentile, so this panel reports the worst node rather than inventing one.
panels.title: Write Latency ${percentile} per Cluster (slowest node, ${latency_unit:text})

panels.description: p50 overlaid with ${percentile} per cluster, both taken from the slowest node. Shows typical and tail latency in one view.
panels.title: Write Latency p50 + ${percentile} per Cluster (slowest node, ${latency_unit:text})

panels.description: Filled band showing the spread between the fastest and slowest node inside each cluster at ${percentile}. A wide band means high node-to-node variance. Works best with a single cluster selected.
panels.title: Write Latency ${percentile} Range (per-node spread, ${latency_unit:text})

panels.description: The whole percentile ladder at once, per node: p50, p99, p999 and max on a log axis. This panel deliberately ignores the $percentile variable — its job is showing the shape of the distribution, not one point on it. The gap between p50 and max is the tail. A log axis keeps all four readable together.
panels.title: Write Latency Percentile Ladder — ${cluster:text} (${latency_unit:text})
5. Activity Matrix — Which cluster was doing what, when

panels.description: Each row = one cluster. Color = throughput tier. Green=low, yellow=medium, blue=high. Best for identifying activity windows across many clusters simultaneously.
panels.title: Throughput Activity by Cluster

panels.description: Each row = one cluster. Red = non-zero errors. Quickly identifies which clusters had error windows and when.
panels.title: Error State by Cluster
6. Percentile Ladder — Full distribution shape per cluster

panels.description: One row per cluster, one column per percentile, each taken from the slowest node in that cluster. Useful for comparing distribution shape: a cluster with a similar p50 but a much higher p999 has a heavier tail. Thresholds assume milliseconds.
panels.title: Latency Percentile Ladder (slowest node per cluster, ${latency_unit:text})

panels.title: Stress Write p99 Latency — $job_name

panels.description: Client-observed read p99 latency per cluster. Pre-computed quantile from the stress job JVM.
panels.title: Stress Read p99 Latency — $job_name

panels.description: Slowest node in each cluster at ${percentile} for reads. The percentile arrives pre-aggregated per node and cannot be recombined into a cluster-wide percentile, so this reports the worst node rather than inventing one.
panels.title: Read Latency ${percentile} per Cluster (slowest node, ${latency_unit:text})

panels.description: p50 overlaid with ${percentile} for reads, both from the slowest node. Shows typical and tail read latency together.
panels.title: Read Latency p50 + ${percentile} per Cluster (slowest node, ${latency_unit:text})

panels.description: Filled band showing the spread between the fastest and slowest node inside each cluster, for reads at ${percentile}. A wide band means high node-to-node variance. Works best with a single cluster selected.
panels.title: Read Latency ${percentile} Range (per-node spread, ${latency_unit:text})

panels.description: The whole read percentile ladder at once, per node: p50, p99, p999 and max on a log axis. This panel deliberately ignores the $percentile variable — its job is the shape of the distribution, not one point on it.
panels.title: Read Latency Percentile Ladder — ${cluster:text} (${latency_unit:text})

panels.description: Bytes read from and written to the block devices of each cluster's database nodes, from the OTel host metrics scraper. Sits beside CPU, memory and network so an I/O-bound cluster is visible next to its other resources.
panels.title: Disk Throughput by Cluster

panels.description: Block device service time at p99, measured in the kernel by ebpf_exporter. This family is a real Prometheus histogram, so histogram_quantile is correct here, unlike the Cassandra latency gauges. It is the storage layer underneath the client latency panels: a jump here explains a jump there.

targets.expr: label_replace(histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, cluster) (rate(ebpf_exporter_bio_latency_seconds_bucket{cluster=~"$cluster", operation="read", host_name=~"$host"}[$__rate_interval]))), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

label_replace(histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, cluster) (rate(ebpf_exporter_bio_latency_seconds_bucket{cluster=~"$cluster", operation="write", host_name=~"$host"}[$__rate_interval]))), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: Block I/O Latency p99 by Cluster
8. JVM and Garbage Collection — pauses, GC time and allocation

panels.description: Share of wall clock time each cluster's nodes spend STOPPED in a GC pause, averaged per node. This is the number that costs you request latency. Concurrent cycles are excluded with jvm_gc_name!~".*Cycles". Compare it with the panel to its right: a concurrent collector moves work out of this panel and into that one, which is the whole point of using one.

targets.expr: label_replace(avg by (cluster) (sum by (cluster, host_name) (rate(jvm_gc_duration_seconds_sum{job="cassandra", jvm_gc_name!~".*Cycles", cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"}[$__rate_interval]))), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: GC Pause Overhead (stop-the-world only)

panels.description: Share of wall clock time spent in any GC activity, averaged per node, with concurrent cycles INCLUDED. This measures CPU the collector consumes, not time the application is stopped. A concurrent collector will read far higher here than in the pause panel to its left, and that is correct, not a regression. Never use this panel to compare collectors on latency.

targets.expr: label_replace(avg by (cluster) (sum by (cluster, host_name) (rate(jvm_gc_duration_seconds_sum{job="cassandra", cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"}[$__rate_interval]))), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: Time Spent in GC (including concurrent work)

panels.description: Stop-the-world pauses per second across each cluster. Read it with the pause duration panel beside it: overhead is rate multiplied by duration, and the two shapes tell you which one moved.
panels.title: GC Pause Rate

panels.description: How long an individual stop-the-world pause lasts. jvm_gc_duration_seconds is a genuine Prometheus histogram, so histogram_quantile is legitimate here — unlike the Cassandra latency gauges, which arrive pre-aggregated. The buckets are wide, so treat these as an order of magnitude rather than an exact figure.

targets.expr: label_replace(histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (le, cluster) (rate(jvm_gc_duration_seconds_bucket{job="cassandra", jvm_gc_name!~".*Cycles", cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"}[$__rate_interval]))), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

label_replace(histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, cluster) (rate(jvm_gc_duration_seconds_bucket{job="cassandra", jvm_gc_name!~".*Cycles", cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"}[$__rate_interval]))), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: GC Pause Duration Percentiles

panels.description: Bytes allocated per second, split into TLAB (thread-local, the fast path) and Main (allocated straight from the heap). Allocation rate is what drives collection frequency, so it is the upstream cause of most GC differences. jvm_memory_allocation_bytes is a histogram; this is the _sum series, and there is no _total. Needs Java 17 or newer: the OpenTelemetry agent derives allocation from JFR and emits no jvm_memory_allocation on Java 11, the default for Cassandra 4.x and 5.0 (run `cassandra use <version> --java 17`).
panels.title: Allocation Rate by Arena

panels.description: The same GC time broken out by collector phase, unfiltered, so you can see which phase dominates. G1 reports Young and Old Generation; generational ZGC reports Major and Minor, each split into Cycles (concurrent) and Pauses (stop-the-world). This is the panel that shows why the two panels above disagree.

targets.expr: label_replace(avg by (cluster, jvm_gc_name) (sum by (cluster, host_name, jvm_gc_name) (rate(jvm_gc_duration_seconds_sum{job="cassandra", cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"}[$__rate_interval]))), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: GC Time by Collector Phase

panels.description: Heap in use against the heap ceiling, averaged per node. The ceiling uses max by (cluster, host_name), never a sum: generational ZGC reports the whole-heap limit on BOTH the young and the old pool, while G1 reports it only on G1 Old Gen, so summing the pools doubles the ceiling on a ZGC node alone.

targets.expr: label_replace(avg by (cluster) (sum by (cluster, host_name) (jvm_memory_used_bytes{jvm_memory_type="heap", job="cassandra", cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"})), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

label_replace(avg by (cluster) (max by (cluster, host_name) (jvm_memory_limit_bytes{jvm_memory_type="heap", job="cassandra", cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"})), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: Heap Used Against the Ceiling

panels.description: Heap still occupied immediately after the last collection, averaged per node. This is the real working set: unlike heap used, it does not include garbage waiting to be collected, so it is the number to watch for a leak or for genuine memory growth under load.

targets.expr: label_replace(avg by (cluster) (sum by (cluster, host_name) (jvm_memory_used_after_last_gc_bytes{jvm_memory_type="heap", job="cassandra", cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"})), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: Live Set After Collection

panels.description: Compaction queue depth against how fast it is draining. A rising backlog with a flat completion rate means compaction cannot keep up, which shows up later as more SSTables per read and worse read latency.
panels.title: Compaction Backlog vs Completion Rate

panels.description: The same backlog attributed to a table, so a single hot table is distinguishable from a cluster-wide problem. System and sidecar keyspaces are excluded.

targets.expr: label_replace(sum by (cluster, keyspace, table) (cassandra_table_compaction_pending{keyspace!~"system.*|sidecar_internal", cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"}), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: Pending Compactions by Table

panels.description: How many SSTables a read touches at p99. This is the mechanical cause behind most read latency differences, and the first thing to check when the read latency panels diverge between clusters. This gauge has no p999, so it does not follow the Percentile picker.

targets.expr: label_replace(max by (cluster, keyspace, table) (cassandra_table_sstables_per_read_p99{keyspace!~"system.*|sidecar_internal", cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"}), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: SSTables per Read p99

panels.description: The five most backed-up thread pools. Pending work here is queueing inside Cassandra and is the usual cause when latency rises without any change in disk or CPU.

targets.expr: label_replace(topk by (cluster) (5, sum by (cluster, pool) (cassandra_thread_pool_tasks_pending{cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"})), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: Thread Pool Pending (top 5)

panels.description: Messages the node gave up on rather than processed. Any sustained non-zero value here means the cluster is shedding work, and a latency comparison against a cluster that is not shedding work is not a fair one.

targets.expr: label_replace(topk by (cluster) (5, sum by (cluster, message_type) (rate(cassandra_messages_dropped_total{cluster=~"$cluster", host_name=~"$host"}[$__rate_interval]))), "cluster_name", "$1", "cluster", "(.+-[0-9a-f]{8})-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}")

panels.title: Dropped Messages by Type (top 5)

panels.description: Hints being replayed, and the rate at which new ones are stored. Hints accrue when a replica is unreachable or too slow to accept a write, so a rising accrual rate marks the moment a cluster started failing writes internally.
panels.title: Hints in Progress and Accrual Rate

title: Experiment: Cassandra

list.description: How far back to look for runs.
list.label: Lookback
list.name: lookback

list.description: The step, in seconds, at which each run's first and last up sample is found.
list.label: Resolution
list.name: resolution

list.description: The home tenant: the tenant of a cluster from before the experiment label when Mimir names none. The installer fills it.
list.name: home_tenant

list.definition: query_result(sort_desc(max by (exp_key, exp_text) (label_join(label_join(max_over_time(timestamp(count by (edl_tenant, experiment) (up{experiment!=""}))[$lookback:${resolution}s]), "exp_key", "/", "edl_tenant", "experiment"), "exp_text", "/", "edl_tenant", "experiment") or label_join(label_join(label_replace(label_replace(max_over_time(timestamp(count by (cluster, __tenant_id__) (up{experiment="", cluster!=""}))[$lookback:${resolution}s]), "t", "$1", "__tenant_id__", "(.+)"), "t", "${home_tenant}", "t", ""), "exp_key", "/", "t", "cluster"), "exp_text", "/", "t", "cluster") or label_replace(label_replace(vector(0), "exp_key", ".*/.*", "", ""), "exp_text", "All", "", ""))))
list.description: An experiment of the tenant view, as <tenant>/<name>, newest first. A cluster from before the experiment label is an experiment of one, named for the cluster. All, the last option, lists every cluster of the tenant view and must be picked by hand.
list.label: Experiment
list.name: experiment
list.query: query_result(sort_desc(max by (exp_key, exp_text) (label_join(label_join(max_over_time(timestamp(count by (edl_tenant, experiment) (up{experiment!=""}))[$lookback:${resolution}s]), "exp_key", "/", "edl_tenant", "experiment"), "exp_text", "/", "edl_tenant", "experiment") or label_join(label_join(label_replace(label_replace(max_over_time(timestamp(count by (cluster, __tenant_id__) (up{experiment="", cluster!=""}))[$lookback:${resolution}s]), "t", "$1", "__tenant_id__", "(.+)"), "t", "${home_tenant}", "t", ""), "exp_key", "/", "t", "cluster"), "exp_text", "/", "t", "cluster") or label_replace(label_replace(vector(0), "exp_key", ".*/.*", "", ""), "exp_text", "All", "", ""))))

list.definition: query_result(max by (cluster) (max_over_time(timestamp(count by (cluster) (up{edl_tenant=~"$exp_tenant", experiment=~"$exp_name"}) or count by (cluster) (up{experiment="", cluster=~"$exp_name"}))[$lookback:${resolution}s])))
list.description: The clusters of the selected experiment with up samples within Lookback. All is the experiment's clusters.
list.label: Cluster
list.name: cluster
list.query: query_result(max by (cluster) (max_over_time(timestamp(count by (cluster) (up{edl_tenant=~"$exp_tenant", experiment=~"$exp_name"}) or count by (cluster) (up{experiment="", cluster=~"$exp_name"}))[$lookback:${resolution}s])))

list.description: Derived from a Cassandra-only metric, so it lists database nodes only and can never offer control0 or app0. host_name is carried by every exporter, so the same filter also works on the system panels. Listed over Lookback, so the hosts of a past experiment are offered.
list.label: Host
list.name: host

list.description: Which pre-aggregated percentile to read. Cassandra emits these as gauges from its own EstimatedHistogram, so there is no bucket to re-aggregate and no cluster-wide percentile to compute.
list.label: Percentile
list.name: percentile

list.description: Display scale for the latency panels. The metric is emitted in microseconds and this value is the multiplier applied in the query. Those panels use the short unit and name the scale in the title, so nothing is converted twice.
list.label: Latency unit
list.name: latency_unit
